propositions.text: On October 17, 2009, the Ocean Lady was apprehended off Vancouver Island with 76 Tamil passengers from Sri Lanka seeking refugee status without legal documentation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that on October 17, 2009, the Ocean Lady was apprehended with 76 Tamil asylum-seekers lacking legal documentation.

propositions.text: The Crown claims the four appellants were organizers of the voyage and that most passengers paid $30,000 to $40,000 for it.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown alleges the four appellants organized the voyage and that most passengers paid $30,000 to $40,000 each.

propositions.text: The appellants were charged under s. 117 of IRPA for organizing illegal entry, with possible imprisonment and refugee disqualification.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellants were charged under s. 117 IRPA for organizing illegal entry, risking imprisonment and refugee disqualification.

propositions.text: The appellants challenged s. 117 IRPA as infringing s. 7 Charter rights to life, liberty, and security.
The trial judge ruled s. 117 unconstitutional for criminalizing family and humanitarian assistance.
The BC Court of Appeal reversed and found s. 117 constitutional.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argued s. 117 infringed s. 7 Charter rights; trial judge found it unconstitutional, but BC Court of Appeal reversed that.

propositions.text: Section 117 is unconstitutional insofar as it permits prosecution for humanitarian aid, mutual asylum-seeker assistance, or family assistance.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 117 is unconstitutional when it permits prosecution for humanitarian, mutual, or family assistance.

propositions.text: Ocean Lady was intercepted with 76 Tamil asylum-seekers from Sri Lanka who boarded in Indonesia and Thailand without proper documentation.
Most migrants agreed to pay $30,000 to $40,000, with $5,000 down payments before boarding and debts after arrival.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Ocean Lady had 76 Tamil asylum-seekers without documents who agreed to pay $30,000-$40,000 for the voyage.

propositions.text: The four appellants are alleged organizers and chief crew of a for-profit smuggling operation from Southeast Asia to Canada.
Appellants held roles: Handasamy as captain, Thevarajah as chief engineer, Kanagarajah and Appulonappa as key crew members.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellants were alleged organizers and chief crew of the smuggling operation with specific roles.

propositions.text: Appellants charged under s. 117(1) IRPA prohibiting knowingly organizing or aiding entry of persons without required documents.

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellants were charged under s. 117(1) IRPA prohibiting organizing or aiding undocumented entry.

propositions.text: IRPA s. 117 was amended in 2012; the version at the time of offences is no longer in force and current constitutionality is not before the court.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 117 was amended in 2012; the version at issue is no longer in force and current constitutionality is not before the court.

propositions.text: Appellants applied for a declaration that s. 117 is unconstitutionally overbroad on a voir dire before Silverman J.
They argued s. 117 may convict humanitarian workers or family members assisting asylum-seekers, exceeding legislative intent and infringing s. 7 liberty.
They submitted this violation was not justified under s. 1 Charter.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants applied for a declaration that s. 117 is overbroad, arguing it may convict humanitarian or family helpers, violating s. 7 and unjustified under s. 1.

propositions.text: The Crown accepted s. 117's purpose excludes convicting family or humanitarian aid providers but argued s. 117(4) consent screens such prosecutions.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown accepted s. 117 excludes convicting family or humanitarian aid but argued s. 117(4) consent prevents improper prosecutions.

propositions.text: Silverman J. found s. 117's purpose excludes prosecuting genuine humanitarian or family aid but s. 117 permits such prosecution, violating s. 7 by overbreadth.
s. 117 cannot be read down to comply with Charter; s. 117(4) consent does not save it from overbreadth.
Overbreadth was not justified under s. 1 Charter.
Silverman J. declared s. 117 inconsistent with s. 7 Charter and ordered appellants' indictments quashed.

paragraphs.summary: Silverman J. found s. 117 overbroad and unconstitutional, not saved by consent, and quashed appellants' indictments.

propositions.text: Before Court of Appeal, Crown changed position, submitting s. 117 aims to prevent all organizing or assisting unlawful entry, including family and humanitarian aid.
This furthers goals of controlling entry, protecting Canadians, preserving immigration integrity, and promoting international justice.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown changed position, arguing s. 117 prevents all unlawful entry assistance, including family and humanitarian aid, to further multiple goals.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal accepted Crown's revised purpose and held s. 117 constitutional.
Canadian laws historically do not exempt offenders based on motive; Parliament rejected humanitarian exceptions in 1988 due to definitional difficulties.
s. 117's purpose aligns with its reach; provision is not overbroad.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal accepted Crown's purpose, found no humanitarian exceptions historically, and held s. 117 constitutional and not overbroad.

propositions.text: s. 117(4) Attorney General consent guards against improper prosecutions on humanitarian or family grounds.
Improper prosecution of humanitarian or family aid would be ministerial discretion abuse, not s. 117(1) overbreadth.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found s. 117(4) consent guards against improper prosecutions; improper prosecutions would be ministerial discretion abuse, not overbreadth.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal allowed appeal, overturned invalidity declaration, set aside acquittals, and remitted for trial.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, overturned invalidity, set aside acquittals, and remitted for trial.

propositions.text: IRPA governs entry of foreign nationals via immigration and refugee protection processes, aiming for fair, efficient procedures and upholding human rights.
Canada's adherence to international conventions underpins IRPA's goals.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA governs immigration and refugee entry aiming for fair procedures and human rights, underpinned by international conventions.

propositions.text: IRPA addresses threat of unauthorized entry outside lawful refugee regime by sanctioning helpers of undocumented entry.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA sanctions individuals helping unauthorized entry to protect refugee system integrity.

propositions.text: Section 37(1)(b) renders inadmissible persons engaged in transnational people smuggling, barring refugee claim merits.
Section 117 creates an offence for knowingly organizing or aiding entry of persons without required documents.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 37(1)(b) bars inadmissible people smugglers from refugee claims; s. 117 creates offence for organizing undocumented entry.

propositions.text: Sections 117(2) and (3) provide penalties; s. 121(1)(c) considers profit as aggravating factor in sentencing under s. 117.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 117(2) and (3) provide penalties; s. 121(1)(c) considers profit an aggravating sentencing factor.

propositions.text: Subsection (4) requires Attorney General's consent to institute proceedings under s. 117.

paragraphs.summary: Subsection (4) requires Attorney General's consent to institute proceedings under s. 117, says the court.

propositions.text: Unauthorized entry participation may lead to prosecution under s. 117 or inadmissibility under s. 37(1)(b).
This appeal concerns prosecution under s. 117; inadmissibility is addressed in companion appeals.

paragraphs.summary: The court states unauthorized entry can lead to prosecution under s. 117 or inadmissibility; this appeal concerns prosecution under s. 117.

propositions.text: Charter applies to foreign nationals entering Canada without required documents: Singh case.
Section 7 of the Charter protects life, liberty, and security of the person except in accordance with fundamental justice.
Section 117 of IRPA threatens liberty and engages s. 7 of the Charter due to potential life imprisonment.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Charter applies to undocumented foreign nationals; s. 7 protects liberty; s. 117 threatens liberty engaging s. 7.

propositions.text: Does s. 117 of IRPA violate s. 7 of the Charter by threatening liberty contrary to fundamental justice?
If yes, is the infringement justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
If not justified, what is the appropriate remedy for s. 117's constitutional infirmity?

paragraphs.summary: The court frames issues: whether s. 117 violates s. 7, if justified under s. 1, and the remedy if not.

propositions.text: s. 117 violates s. 7 because it catches people assisting family or humanitarians outside its purpose, making it overbroad.
s. 117 is grossly disproportionate, unconstitutionally vague, and perpetuates inequality, violating fundamental justice.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue s. 117 violates s. 7 by overbreadth, gross disproportionality, vagueness, and perpetuating inequality.

propositions.text: Overbreadth occurs when law interferes with conduct unrelated to its objective: Bedford and Carter cases.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains overbreadth as law interfering with conduct unrelated to its objective, citing Bedford and Carter.

propositions.text: Overbreadth inquiry: determine law's object, then if it deprives rights in cases not furthering that object.

paragraphs.summary: The court states overbreadth inquiry involves determining law's object and if it deprives rights beyond that object.

propositions.text: s. 117 is overbroad as applied to reasonably foreseeable situations beyond the appellants' conduct.
Courts may consider reasonable hypotheticals to assess Charter consistency: Nur case.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue s. 117 is overbroad in foreseeable situations; courts may consider hypotheticals per Nur case.

propositions.text: First scenario: assisting close family members to flee to Canada is caught by s. 117 overbroadly.
Mutual assistance among asylum-seekers is similar and reasonably foreseeable.
Refugees assisting each other is not meaningfully different from family assistance; companion case B010 confirms foreseeability.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue s. 117 overbroadly catches family and mutual asylum assistance; court finds this foreseeable and similar.

propositions.text: Second scenario: humanitarian aid to fleeing persecuted people is caught by s. 117 overbroadly.
Humanitarian aid by individuals or groups to refugees is a past and current reality, supported by parliamentary debate.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue s. 117 overbroadly catches humanitarian aid; court notes humanitarian aid is real and documented.

propositions.text: Overbreadth analysis depends on whether law's reach exceeds its object; first step is determining s. 117's object.

paragraphs.summary: The court states overbreadth analysis starts by determining s. 117's object to see if law's reach exceeds it.

propositions.text: Crown says s. 117's purpose is to catch all acts assisting undocumented migrants; thus not overbroad.
Appellants say 'human smuggling' has narrower purpose; s. 117 is overbroad catching all assistance acts.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues s. 117 targets all assistance to undocumented migrants; appellants say purpose is narrower, making it overbroad.

propositions.text: Determining legislative purpose requires considering text, context, statements, and international law.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains legislative purpose is determined by text, context, statements, and international law.

propositions.text: Court agrees with appellants that s. 117's purpose is narrower than Crown asserts, focused on combating people smuggling.
Text is broad but purpose emerges from international instruments, statute context, IRPA purpose, evolution, and debates.
'People smuggling' excludes humanitarian conduct, mutual assistance, or family aid per companion case B010.
s. 117 violates Charter by catching conduct outside its purpose.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117's purpose is narrower, targeting people smuggling, excluding humanitarian and family aid, thus violating Charter by overreach.

propositions.text: Text of s. 117(1) prohibits knowingly organizing, inducing, aiding, or abetting entry of persons without required documents.
Penalties vary by number of persons involved, with fines and imprisonment up to life.
No proceedings without Attorney General's consent per s. 117(4).

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes s. 117's text: broad prohibition on aiding undocumented entry, penalties vary by group size, and consent required.

propositions.text: All agree s. 117(1) text is broad enough to catch family and humanitarian assistance.
Overbreadth doctrine recognizes state may use broader means than necessary to achieve legitimate objective.
Overbreadth requires courts to look beyond text to legislative purpose when law is instrumentally irrational: Bedford, Carter, Heywood.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes s. 117(1) is broad but overbreadth doctrine allows courts to look beyond text to legislative purpose.

propositions.text: Marginal note and subheading suggest s. 117 targets smuggling in organized crime, not humanitarian or family assistance.
Marginal notes have limited weight in statutory interpretation: Sullivan.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117's marginal note and subheading suggest focus on organized crime smuggling, not humanitarian or family aid.

propositions.text: Increased sanctions for groups of 10+ persons suggest focus on large-scale smuggling operations.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds harsher penalties for large groups indicate focus on large-scale smuggling.

propositions.text: Requirement of Attorney General's consent suggests s. 117 not intended to convict all who fall within broad ambit.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Attorney General's consent requirement suggests s. 117 not meant to convict everyone caught by broad text.

propositions.text: Legislation presumed to comply with Canada's international obligations; courts interpret accordingly.
IRPA s. 3 requires interpretation consistent with international human rights instruments Canada has signed.

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislation is presumed to comply with international obligations; IRPA requires interpretation consistent with human rights instruments.

propositions.text: IRPA provisions on unauthorized entry assisting respond to Canada's international commitments in Refugee Convention, UN Organized Crime Convention, Smuggling Protocol, and Trafficking Protocol.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA provisions on unauthorized entry assisting respond to Canada's international commitments in various international conventions.

propositions.text: Refugee Convention prohibits penalties for illegal entry of refugees who come directly from threatened territories and present themselves promptly with good cause.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Refugee Convention prohibits penalties for illegal entry of refugees who come directly from threatened territories and present themselves promptly with good cause.

propositions.text: Section 133 IRPA protects foreign nationals entering without documents from illegal entry charges while refugee claims are pending.
Article 31(1) Refugee Convention provides immunity for genuine refugees entering illegally to seek refuge, including collective illegal entry assistance.
States cannot criminalize refugees solely for aiding others to enter illegally in collective flight to safety under art. 31(1).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 133 IRPA protects undocumented refugees during claims, and art. 31(1) Refugee Convention forbids criminalizing refugees aiding others' illegal entry in collective flight.

propositions.text: Smuggling Protocol aims to stop organized people smuggling, requiring criminalization of smuggling for financial or material benefit.
Smuggling Protocol excludes family members or humanitarians from its scope and includes a saving clause preserving other international rights.
Crown's broad interpretation of s. 117 conflicts with Smuggling Protocol's protection of smuggled migrants' rights.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Smuggling Protocol targets organized smuggling for profit, excludes family/humanitarian aid, and Crown's broad s. 117 interpretation conflicts with it.

propositions.text: Interpretation harmonizing Canada's international obligations supports s. 117 targeting organized crime, excluding humanitarian, mutual, or family aid.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes harmonizing international obligations supports s. 117 targeting organized crime, excluding humanitarian, mutual, or family aid.

propositions.text: Section 117 IRPA must be read harmoniously with other IRPA provisions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 117 IRPA must be read harmoniously with other IRPA provisions.

propositions.text: Section 117 IRPA is under Part 3 'Enforcement' and subheading 'Human Smuggling and Trafficking'; s. 118 creates human trafficking offence; s. 37(1)(b) renders inadmissible persons engaged in smuggling or trafficking.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 117 IRPA is under enforcement for human smuggling; s. 118 creates trafficking offence; s. 37(1)(b) bars inadmissible persons engaged in smuggling or trafficking.

propositions.text: Section 37(1)(b) IRPA conduct matches Smuggling Protocol's definition of people smuggling for financial benefit in transnational crime context.
Reading IRPA inadmissibility and enforcement provisions harmoniously shows s. 117 targets organized smuggling for financial benefit, excluding humanitarian, mutual, or family aid.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 37(1)(b) matches Smuggling Protocol's people smuggling for profit, so s. 117 targets organized smuggling for financial benefit, excluding humanitarian, mutual, or family aid.

propositions.text: Legislative purpose is best found in statements of purpose in the legislation itself.

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislative purpose is best found in statements of purpose in the legislation itself.

propositions.text: Febles v. Canada holds Refugee Convention aims to provide humanitarian refuge while protecting states' borders.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Febles v. Canada that Refugee Convention aims to provide humanitarian refuge while protecting states' borders.

propositions.text: IRPA's object provisions show both humanitarian refuge and border security goals are important, so s. 117 must be balanced accordingly.
Whether s. 117 should be interpreted to allow security concerns to override humanitarian aims.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes IRPA's objects require balancing humanitarian and security goals in s. 117 interpretation, raising issue of security overriding humanitarian aims.

propositions.text: Crown argues s. 117 aims to catch all assistance to undocumented migrants to protect security, health, and safety.
IRPA objectives include border control for security, health, and safety, including denying access to security risks and protecting Canadians.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues s. 117 aims to catch all assistance to undocumented migrants for security; the court notes IRPA objectives include border control for security and safety.

propositions.text: 1988 amendments to Immigration Act added purposes including preserving access for genuine protection seekers, controlling abuse of refugee claims, deterring illegal entry assistance, and responding to security concerns.

paragraphs.summary: The court states 1988 amendments added purposes including preserving genuine protection access, controlling refugee claim abuse, deterring illegal entry assistance, and addressing security concerns.

propositions.text: The 1988 statute also recognized humanitarian commitments and concern for exploitation and risks to migrants.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the 1988 statute recognized humanitarian commitments and concern for exploitation and risks to migrants.

propositions.text: IRPA's general objects include Canada's humanitarian ideals, saving lives, offering protection, and complying with international human rights instruments.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA's general objects include humanitarian ideals, saving lives, protection, and compliance with international human rights instruments.

propositions.text: IRPA includes commitment to family reunification as a stated object.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA includes commitment to family reunification as a stated object.

propositions.text: Security goals of IRPA do not supplant humanitarian aid and family unity; s. 117 targets organized smuggling with criminal dimension, excluding humanitarian, mutual, and family aid.
Crown's interpretation would criminalize trivial humanitarian acts, incompatible with IRPA's refugee protection objects.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes IRPA's security goals do not override humanitarian and family aims; s. 117 targets organized smuggling, excluding humanitarian aid, unlike Crown's broad interpretation.

propositions.text: Legislative history may assist in determining a provision's purpose.

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislative history may assist in determining a provision's purpose.

propositions.text: Canada has criminalized assisting undocumented migrants since 1902, initially focusing on organizing illegal arrival by rail or ship with little concern for migrants' plight.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Canada criminalized assisting undocumented migrants since 1902, focusing on organizing illegal arrival by rail or ship with little concern for migrants.

propositions.text: In 1919, it was an offence to transport, harbour, or conceal prohibited immigrants with penalties of imprisonment or fines; similar offences existed in 1952 and 1976 Immigration Acts.

paragraphs.summary: The court states 1919 law criminalized transporting or harbouring prohibited immigrants with penalties; similar offences existed in 1952 and 1976 Acts.

propositions.text: In 1988, amendments introduced a new offence criminalizing third party assistance to undocumented migrants, now s. 117 of the IRPA.
Maximum penalties varied by number of undocumented entrants, with harsher penalties for 10 or more entrants.
The offence included a screening mechanism requiring Attorney General's consent for proceedings under certain sections.
Greater culpability attached to large-scale breaches reflecting greater organizational activity.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the 1988 amendments creating s. 117, criminalizing third party assistance to undocumented migrants with penalties and a screening mechanism.

propositions.text: The current s. 117 was enacted in 2001 as part of the IRPA, preserving penalties and screening mechanisms.
Maximum penalties were increased and s. 121 was added to guide sentencing considering harm, criminal association, profit, and treatment of migrants.
These changes followed the Smuggling Protocol requiring criminalization of smuggling for financial benefit and aggravating circumstances.
The factors in s. 121 reflect links to organized crime and recognition of more serious crime.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the 2001 IRPA enactment of s. 117, increasing penalties and adding sentencing factors reflecting organized crime and harm.

propositions.text: Prohibitions have focused on smuggling tied to organizing illegal entry, not incidental aid.
Revisions increased penalties and targeted organized crime-related smuggling, aligning with international law.
Section 117 filters out assistance not associated with organized criminal smuggling, like humanitarian acts and family aid.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes prohibitions target organized smuggling, penalties increased over time, and s. 117 filters out innocent humanitarian and family aid.

propositions.text: Legislative statements may supply evidence of a provision's purpose, citing authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislative statements can evidence a provision's purpose, citing case law.

propositions.text: Parliamentary debates show the 1988 offence was motivated by organized large-scale smuggling by sea.
Debates expressed concerns about protecting Canadians, immigration integrity, border control, and refugee safety.
Minister Bouchard summarized Parliament's purpose to stop large-scale trafficking and avoid loopholes undermining prosecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts 1988 parliamentary debates showing the offence aimed at stopping large-scale smuggling and protecting various interests.

propositions.text: Section 117(1) permits prosecution of humanitarian and family assistance due to drafting dilemmas, not intent to capture such persons.
Parliament sought to screen out humanitarian and mutual aid at prosecution stage via Attorney General's consent, not by exemption.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117(1) permits prosecution of humanitarian and family aid due to drafting, relying on Attorney General consent to screen.

propositions.text: 2001 debates echoed concerns about criminalizing family and humanitarian aid under s. 117.
Government responded that s. 117(4) requiring Attorney General consent would prevent unintended prosecutions.
Excerpts from debates show officials explaining the safeguard role of s. 117(4) and prosecutorial discretion.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes 2001 debates where government assured s. 117(4) would prevent prosecution of family and humanitarian aid providers.

propositions.text: Parliament understood s. 117(1) criminalized family and humanitarian aid but relied on Attorney General discretion as a safeguard.
Officials defended overreach on basis that Attorney General's permission would prevent inappropriate prosecutions.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament accepted s. 117(1) criminalized family and humanitarian aid but relied on Attorney General discretion as safeguard.

propositions.text: Government conceded s. 117(1) was broad enough to catch family and humanitarian aid but did not intend to prosecute them.
Attorney General authorization under s. 117(4) was asserted to alleviate prosecution risk.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes government conceded s. 117(1) was overbroad but relied on Attorney General authorization to prevent prosecutions.

propositions.text: Section 117's purpose is to criminalize organized crime-related smuggling, not family or humanitarian aid.
A broad punitive goal prosecuting persons unconnected to organized crime is inconsistent with Parliament's purpose.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 117 targets organized crime smuggling and does not intend to prosecute family or humanitarian aid.

propositions.text: Whether s. 117 goes too far and interferes with conduct unrelated to its objective.

paragraphs.summary: The court raises the issue whether s. 117 overreaches by interfering with conduct unrelated to its objective.

propositions.text: Section 117(1) is unambiguous and admits no ambiguity in its scope.
Parliament knew s. 117(1) caught humanitarian, mutual and family assistance but relied on Attorney General not to prosecute them.
Interpreting s. 117(1) to exclude prosecution of humanitarian, mutual or family aid would ignore ordinary meaning and legislative record.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117(1) unambiguous and overbroad, catching humanitarian and family aid, relying on Attorney General discretion.

propositions.text: Section 117(1) criminalizes some conduct unrelated to its objective, raising overbreadth concerns.
Whether Attorney General's consent under s. 117(4) cures the overbreadth by narrowing s. 117(1)'s scope.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117(1) overbroad and questions if Attorney General consent under s. 117(4) cures this overbreadth.

propositions.text: Section 117(4) does not cure overbreadth; ministerial discretion does not negate criminalization beyond Parliament's object.
Persons assisting family or providing humanitarian aid face risk of prosecution and imprisonment under s. 117.
Possibility of prosecution under s. 117 engages s. 7 of the Charter.
Prosecutorial discretion does not excuse constitutional breaches (R. v. Anderson).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117(4) does not cure overbreadth; risk of prosecution engages s. 7; prosecutorial discretion cannot excuse breaches.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal viewed problem as administrative law issue about Attorney General's discretion under s. 117(4).
Court disagrees; s. 117 allows prosecution of unintended persons and judicial review of discretion is limited and undesirable.
Judicial review of prosecutorial discretion is limited to preserve adversarial system roles (R. v. Anderson).

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects Court of Appeal's administrative law view, noting limited judicial review of prosecutorial discretion under s. 117(4).

propositions.text: Judicial review of Attorney General's decision under s. 117(4) may have undesirable consequences for other federal statutes with similar clauses.
Judicial review does not resolve constitutional non-conformity of s. 117(1).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes judicial review under s. 117(4) may affect other statutes and does not fix s. 117(1)'s constitutional issues.

propositions.text: Section 117 of the IRPA is overbroad.
Whether the overbreadth is justified under s. 1 of the Charter.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 117 is overbroad and raises the issue of justification under s. 1 of the Charter.

propositions.text: Section 117 offends s. 7 by gross disproportionality, vagueness, and violates equality under law.
Given s. 117 is overbroad, court finds it unnecessary to consider these additional arguments.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues s. 117 violates s. 7 and equality; the court finds these need not be considered due to overbreadth.

propositions.text: The s. 1 justification test is from R. v. Oakes, requiring pressing and substantial objective.
The broad purpose of s. 117 is to combat organized crime-related people smuggling without criminalizing family or humanitarian aid.
This objective is pressing and substantial.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the s. 1 test from Oakes and finds s. 117's purpose pressing and substantial.

propositions.text: Not all applications of s. 117 are rationally connected to its objective; it catches humanitarian and family aid.
Other applications are rationally connected, satisfying the rational connection stage of s. 1 analysis.
Rational connection requires only some applications to be connected, not complete correspondence (Heywood).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117 partly rationally connected to its objective, satisfying s. 1's rational connection stage.

propositions.text: The third step of s. 1 analysis asks if the law is tailored to its objective, citing R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd.
A law that goes too far challenges minimal impairment requirement.
In Heywood, Cory J. found the law overly broad and failing minimal impairment under s. 1.
The record here shows that failing minimal impairment will not always be the case for overbroad laws.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 1 minimal impairment step, cites Heywood's finding of overbroad law failing minimal impairment, but notes this is not always so.

propositions.text: The Crown argues the overbroad provision is still minimally impairing as no better alternative existed.
Government knew provision would catch unintended conduct but enacted it to avoid loopholes.
Section 1 requires demonstrable justification for rights limits, not bare claims, citing Oakes.
The Crown has not met its burden under s. 1 to justify the provision.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues minimal impairment despite overbreadth; the court finds no justification and rejects the Crown's position under s. 1.

propositions.text: Section 52(1) of Constitution Act, 1982 states constitution is supreme and inconsistent laws are of no force.
Section 117 is of no force to the extent it conflicts with the Charter.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 52(1) supremacy and that s. 117 is invalid to the extent it conflicts with the Charter.

propositions.text: The inconsistency proven is s. 117's overbreadth regarding humanitarian aid, mutual aid among asylum-seekers, and family assistance.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117 overbroad in three conduct categories: humanitarian aid, mutual aid, and family assistance.

propositions.text: The appellants ask to strike down s. 117 entirely.
Section 117 was replaced after the alleged offences.
The preferable remedy is to read down s. 117 to exclude humanitarian, mutual, and family assistance conduct.
This remedy aligns with Schachter v. Canada guidance and preserves human smuggling prohibition.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants seek full strike down; court prefers reading down s. 117 to exclude certain aid, consistent with Schachter.

propositions.text: Appeals allowed; s. 117 read down to exclude humanitarian and mutual aid to conform with Charter.
Charges remitted for trial on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows appeals, reads down s. 117 excluding humanitarian and mutual aid, and remits charges for trial.
